title: Ice Cube Fires Back at Dejon Paul Over LA Rappers
htmlContent:
Ice Cube has spent more than three decades building one of the most diverse résumés in entertainment, from N.W.A and a platinum solo career to Hollywood franchises and his own professional basketball league. But rapper and YouTube personality Dejon Paul recently questioned what the West Coast icon has done for the next generation of Los Angeles rappers, and the exchange quickly turned into a heated back-and-forth on X involving Cube and his son, actor O'Shea Jackson Jr.

A Drakeo Debate Sparks the Feud

The dispute began at ComplexCon, where Paul interviewed Ralfy The Plug. During the conversation, the two agreed that the late Drakeo The Ruler would have outsold AZ Chike if he had major-label support behind him.

Jackson Jr. took issue with the comparison, questioning why Chike needed to be diminished to make the point.

"What's the point of tryna tear AzChike down tho. Why not just talk about how big Drakeo would've been with a major behind him."

Dejon Paul Turns the Focus to Ice Cube

Paul pushed back, insisting he wasn't criticizing Chike. He then shifted the conversation to Jackson Jr.'s father.

"No one is tearing AzChike down, I said LA rap needs another game changer like Drakeo and his fans said he couldn't outsell Chike. More importantly, why hasn't your father @IceCube w/ all his multi-millions and resources signed or developed any new LA rappers this decade or last?"

At its core, Paul's criticism was about mentorship. He argued that an artist with Cube's wealth and industry connections should be investing in emerging local talent. Jackson Jr. defended his father by pointing to the decades of opportunities Cube has created across music, film and sports.

Ice Cube Responds

Cube caught wind of the comments and issued a lengthy response, laying out everything currently on his plate.

"Because I'm an independent artist who's not retired or semiretired. I write, produce and perform my own music. I write, produce, direct and star in movies. I also produce the soundtracks. I produce television as well. I'm also the co-founder and CEO of my own professional basketball league called the BIG3. It's unfair for any rapper to be signed to me and expect the kind of attention they need to be successful."

I produce television as well. I'm also the co-founder and CEO of my own professional basketball league called the BIG3. It's unfair for any rapper to be signed to me and expect the kind of attention they need to be successful. People like you, will always criticize people like me for not using my talents and resources in the way they see fit. Mind your own business cause the first time something is produced that you consider "wack" you'd be asking everybody "Why'd they working with an old ass nigga like Cube!?" Stop trying to cause problems in L.A. and keep it pushing.

— Ice Cube (@icecube) October 5, 2026

Cube added that critics will always question how artists like him use their talents and resources. He told Paul to mind his own business, predicting that the first time Cube produced something Paul considered "wack," Paul would be asking why anyone was working with an old-timer like him. He closed with a warning: "Stop trying to cause problems in L.A. and keep it pushing."

Things Get Personal

Rather than cooling off, the exchange escalated. Paul questioned Cube's cultural standing, calling him a "buster" and a "studio gangsta." Cube responded by daring Paul to come and try to snatch his chain.

Cube eventually ended the debate on his own terms. He posted Paul's Spotify streaming numbers, then resurfaced an old tweet in which Paul named Ice Cube as one of his West Coast favorites.

Two Different Measures of Contribution

The feud highlights a long-running debate in hip-hop about what established stars owe the next generation. Paul's argument centers on direct investment, signing and developing new recording artists. Cube's defense rests on a broader view of contribution—one that includes creating jobs and opportunities in film, television and the BIG3.

Both claims at the heart of the argument remain matters of opinion. Paul's suggestion that Cube has failed LA's newer artists has not been backed by evidence, and the idea that Drakeo would have outsold Chike with major-label support is a hypothetical that can never be tested.

Cube's Legacy Speaks for Itself

Few artists have had a greater impact on Los Angeles culture than Ice Cube. He helped put West Coast hip-hop on the map with N.W.A, became a bankable movie star with the Friday and Barbershop franchises, and turned the BIG3 into a platform for former NBA players.

Whether that résumé satisfies critics like Paul is another question. But Cube made one thing clear on X: he has no intention of letting anyone else define his contributions to the city he calls home.
excerpt: Ice Cube responded to rapper and YouTube personality Dejon Paul after Paul questioned what the West Coast icon has done to sign or develop new Los Angeles rappers, sparking a heated back-and-forth on X that also drew in Cube's son, actor O'Shea Jackson Jr.
